diagnosis.what_is_wrong: A short, localized CPU burst is visible: python3 in the only non-host namespace used about 2.52 CPU-seconds during a 3-second interval, after recording no CPU in the selected quiet interval. This is consistent with CPU-bound work associated with the coding task, but the trace does not establish that it caused the reported delay or show host-wide CPU pressure; it is not enough to diagnose a host saturation incident.
diagnosis.evidence: ctf_timespan places the recording at 03:21:49.000–03:22:06.400 UTC. Comparing equal 3-second intervals in the worker's run_python sched_stat_runtime aggregates: python3 used 0 ms in 03:21:53–03:21:56, 254.298 ms in 03:21:56–03:21:59, then 2,519.853 ms in 03:21:59–03:22:02, approximately 100 ms in nearly every 100-ms bucket. The worker also reports that scheduler and block event rates had dropped substantially after the opening burst, with no synchronized later recovery, so this does not support a host-wide collapse. The trace identifies only pid_ns 4026531836, not a service name. The notes contain no ctf_lines output, so raw event-field corroboration was not available here.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The selected window is the equal-duration 3-second interval where python3 runtime jumps from 254.298 ms in the immediately preceding interval to 2,519.853 ms, with nearly every 100-ms bucket reaching roughly 100 ms CPU. The earlier 03:21:53–03:21:56 interval had no python3 runtime and provides the worker's quiet comparison. The available aggregates do not justify extending the window beyond this measured burst.
